Everything is Predictable, 2024. The test correctly identifies 90% of the actual positive cases → Recall Out of all positive test results, only 8.3% are true → Precision Is this a bad test? The F1 score is ~15%, which could indicate that it is. But in low-prevalence settings (aka class imbalance), high precision is almost impossible unless the test is nearly perfect. A confusion matrix helps make this more concrete: • Precision = P(YCOVID+ | XTEST+) • Recall = P(XTEST+ | YCOVID+) Precision is the probability of having COVID given a positive test, P(YCOVID+ | XTEST+) = 900 / 10,890 = 0.083 (8.3%). Recall is the class-conditional probability P(XTEST+ | YCOVID+) = 900 / 1,000 = 0.9 (90%). F1 Score = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall) = 2 × (0.083 × 0.9) / (0.083 + 0.9) ≈ 15%. If you tested people at random, and your test correctly identified people who didn’t have Covid 99% of the time, and people who did have Covid 90% of the time, more than 90% of your positives would be false.”

Another look at Precision, Recall, and F1 score Precision acts as a function of prevalence. When prevalence is very low, the denominator becomes dominated by False Positives, and Precision drops sharply. The model’s sensitivity (recall) and specificity (TNR = 1 − FPR) are fixed, while prevalence varies. The model’s ROC AUC score is fixed, while prevalence varies.
